source: Zheng et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs
finding: Two-step prompt: first ask a step-back question to get the governing principle or high-level concept, then answer using it. Large gains on PaLM-2L for physics and chemistry. Gains are smaller on GPT-4 and Llama2-70B.
numbers: MMLU Physics / Chemistry, PaLM-2L: base 66.4 / 70.9; CoT 65.0 / 75.3; Step-Back 73.2 / 81.8 (+7 / +11 over base). GPT-4: base 69.4 / 80.9; CoT 82.9 / 85.3; Step-Back 84.5 / 85.6. Llama2-70B: base 51.9 / 55.7; CoT 59.3 / 64.1; Step-Back 64.8 / 66.7.
limits: On GPT-4 Step-Back is only +1.6 and +0.3 over plain CoT (inside the reported SD of 0.5 to 1.4). Headline gains are a PaLM-2L result. Abstract says TimeQA +27%; the DeepMind page says 34%.
agent_relevance: The principle-first step gives a clear gain over no scaffold, but a strong model with CoT already gets most of it. Test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Zheng et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs
finding: Knowledge QA: step-back alone lifts TimeQA a lot on PaLM-2L, and step-back plus retrieval adds more. Multi-hop: moderate gain on MuSiQue, none on StrategyQA without retrieval.
numbers: TimeQA PaLM-2L: base 41.5, RAG 57.4, Step-Back 66.0, Step-Back+RAG 68.7 (Hard split 40.4 -> 61.6 with Step-Back; RAG alone Hard 46.8). GPT-4 base 45.6. SituatedQA: 54.3 -> 57.5 (Step-Back), 61.0 (+RAG), GPT-4 63.2. MuSiQue: 35.5 -> 42.6; StrategyQA: 82.8 -> 82.7 (Step-Back), 86.4 with RAG. GSM8K PaLM-2L: base 75.8, CoT 84.4, Step-Back 84.3.
limits: On GSM8K and StrategyQA step-back equals CoT or base: no gain where little principle recall is needed. One model family carries the headline numbers.
agent_relevance: Abstraction helps most where the right principle or fact is hard to recall and retrieval can ground the answer. Little value on easy arithmetic or yes/no tasks (G11, G12).

source: Zheng et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs
finding: Error analysis: step-back fixes many baseline errors and breaks few. Most remaining errors are in applying the principle (reasoning or math), not in picking it.
numbers: MMLU high-school Physics: fixes 20.5% of baseline errors, introduces 11.9% new ones. TimeQA: fixes 39.9% of baseline errors, introduces 5.6%; fixes 21.6% of RAG errors, introduces 6.3%. Over 90% of Step-Back errors in physics happen in the Reasoning step; Principle Error is a small share.
quote: Step-Back fixes a large portion of errors of the base model (up to ~40%) while introducing a small portion of new errors (max ~12%).
limits: Error labels are hand annotated by the authors on a sample. The net physics gain hides 11.9% new errors, so the step is not free.
agent_relevance: Getting the principle right is not the bottleneck; applying it is. A schema that only adds a principle step needs a checker for the application step (G2, G3).

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with LLMs
finding: Buffer of Thoughts keeps a meta-buffer of high-level thought-templates distilled from past problems. A problem-distiller extracts the task's key information, the nearest template is retrieved and instantiated. Large gains on tasks with a reusable structure.
numbers: GPT-4, accuracy %: Game of 24: standard 3.0, CoT 11.0, ToT 74.0, BoT 82.4. Checkmate-in-One: 36.4 / 32.8 / 49.2 (ToT) / 86.4. Geometric Shapes: 52.6 / 69.2 / 56.8 / 93.6. Word sorting 80.4 -> 100.0. MGSM 84.4 -> 89.2. Python puzzles 31.1 -> 52.4. Penguins 71.1 -> 94.7 (PAL 93.3). Cost about 12% of multi-query methods (ToT, GoT).
limits: Authors' own benchmark set; templates are seeded per task type and tested on the same task families, so this is within-family transfer. Not independently replicated in what I read.
agent_relevance: A template library built from solved cases is the machine version of a schema. Gains are largest where one structure repeats (Game of 24, chess mate). Fits memory of solved subgoals; must still pass G7.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with LLMs
finding: Ablations: the problem-distiller matters most on hard tasks, and a buffer-manager that updates the template store is what makes accuracy rise across rounds.
numbers: Four-round test: accuracy rises with the buffer-manager and stays flat without it. Removing the problem-distiller hurts Game of 24 and Checkmate-in-One most, MGSM and word sorting least (Llama3-70B and GPT-4).
limits: Bar values only in figures; direction recorded, not exact numbers. Only four benchmarks in the ablation.
agent_relevance: Two design hints: distil the problem to its essentials before retrieving a template, and let the library grow online. Both are cheap code steps (G5).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes K relevant but different example problems with solutions (and, for code, key knowledge) before solving the target. No labeled exemplars needed. It beats 0-shot CoT and often hand-written few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo: 5-shot CoT 75.0, self-generated exemplars 77.8. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.0 -> 37.3; PaLM2 27.1 -> 34.8. Codeforces GPT-3.5-turbo-16k Acc@1: 3-shot CoT 8% -> knowledge+exemplars 15%; GPT-4 16% -> 19%. Average gain about +4% over baselines.
limits: PDF table text was garbled; column mapping for some rows is inferred. Works only with large models: text-curie and davinci-001 do better with retrieved labeled exemplars.
agent_relevance: Self-generated cases are a cheap way to make the model compare cases before solving, but weak models cannot generate valid cases. Gate by model strength and measured gain (G7).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: How many self-generated cases: one case hurts (the model over-relies on it), three to five is best.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K / MATH accuracy by K: 76.1 / 34.8 at K=1 (lowest), 77.0 / 36.7, 77.5 / 37.3 at K=3, 77.3 / 37.0, 77.8 / 37.1 at K=5 (row-to-K mapping read from layout text). Text: K=1 underperforms due to excessive reliance on a single case; K>=3 stable.
limits: Effect is small, 1 to 3 points between K=1 and K=3 to 5.
agent_relevance: Matches the human finding that two or more cases beat one for schema formation: with a single case the model copies its surface. Use at least three varied cases if we generate them.

source: Hong et al. (2024) Abstraction-of-Thought Makes Language Models Better Reasoners
finding: Abstraction-of-Thought (AoT) is a reasoning format with an abstract plan level first, then concrete steps. Fine-tuning on 348k AoT samples beats fine-tuning on CoT-format data.
numbers: BBH zero-shot, 23 unseen tasks: Llama-3-8B-AoT beats Llama-3-8B-CoT by +9.7 absolute. 3-shot prompting, CoT format -> AoT format: Llama-3-8B 60.0 -> 75.1 (+15.1); CodeLlama-7B 41.4 -> 66.0 (+24.6); Llama-2-7B 37.8 -> 56.5 (+18.7); Mistral-7B 55.2 -> 71.0 (+15.8). Fine-tuned models, 3-shot: Llama-3-8B-AoT 82.5 vs Llama-3-8B-CoT 43.9.
limits: Gain is entangled with AoT using Python code for some steps (CodeLlama-7B-AoT code responses 61.1% vs text 43.6%). Ablation with same back-end LLM says format is the main factor. Failure modes: 38% wrong reasoning steps, 16% missing knowledge.
agent_relevance: A format that forces a high-level step before details helps small models a lot, but part of the gain is the move to executable code. Separate the two before claiming an abstraction effect.

source: Hong et al. (2024) Abstraction-of-Thought Makes Language Models Better Reasoners
finding: Training-data ablation: 10k AoT samples already beat 348k CoT samples; AoT responses cost about 80% more tokens than CoT.
numbers: Reasoning-format ablation (10k questions, zero-shot BBH): AoT2CoT 46.1 total, AoT from collection 50.1. 10k AoT data beats 348k CoT data. AoT responses use about 80% more tokens.
limits: Token cost is large; at equal tokens the advantage is smaller. Authors' own dataset.
agent_relevance: Tests G7 directly: the abstraction format pays only if it wins at equal tokens.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: Self-Discover selects, adapts and composes atomic reasoning modules into a task-level reasoning structure once per task type, from a few unlabeled examples, then reuses it for every instance. This is schema induction at task level.
numbers: BBH / T4D / MATH accuracy %: PaLM 2-L base 56/30/45, CoT 60/40/42, Plan-and-Solve 61/42/49, Self-Discover 67/69/50.5. GPT-4 base 58/51/70.5, CoT 75/52/71, PS 73/53/70, Self-Discover 81/85/73. Up to 32% over CoT; 10 to 40x fewer inference calls than CoT-Self-Consistency.
limits: T4D (theory-of-mind agent task) is the headline gain; BBH gain over CoT is 6 to 7 points; MATH gain 1 to 7 points. 74.7% of MATH failures are arithmetic errors, not wrong structures. Structures correct in 87.5% of 200 checked examples.
agent_relevance: Per-task-type structure discovery is cheap and reused for every instance. Good model for a once-per-class schema step; gains concentrate in algorithmic tasks.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: Structures transfer across model families: a structure discovered by a strong model helps weaker models.
numbers: Llama2 with self-discovered structures 52% vs CoT 42% on disambiguation QA zero-shot; GPT-3.5-turbo 56% vs 51% on geometric shapes. Mean BBH gain over CoT: +11% (PaLM 2-L), +7% (GPT-4).
limits: Transfer examples are on a few tasks; no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Supports a cached schema library built once by a strong model and applied cheaply by a weaker one.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students on zero-shot text matrix reasoning, letter-string, verbal and story analogies. Its difficulty pattern followed human patterns (relational complexity, spatial alignment).
numbers: Digit Matrices: GPT-3 above human mean, OR 1.88, p=0.005, 95% CI [1.21, 2.91] (human N=40). Item-type difficulty correlation human vs GPT-3 r(30)=0.39, p=0.027. Human Ns: letter-string 57, verbal analogy 57, story analogy 54. Preliminary GPT-4 higher.
limits: Zero-shot analogy solving between given items, not building a schema from several cases. Training-set contamination cannot be excluded (see Hodel and West; Lewis and Mitchell).
agent_relevance: Base evidence that models can do structure mapping when it is spelled out. Does not show they induce a schema from several cases.

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Small changes to the letter-string task break GPT-3 while humans stay accurate. Authors argue the original success came from familiar real-alphabet problems seen in training data.
numbers: Humans N=121 UW undergraduates: accuracy on modified (larger interval, synthetic alphabet) problems about the same as original. GPT-3, N=50 instances per type: accuracy falls for 5 of 6 problem types; only 'remove redundant letter' holds, and 'sort' is similar to the original. A counterfactual comprehension check shows GPT-3 can read the synthetic alphabet.
limits: GPT-3 only; results are in charts, so exact percentages not recorded. Conclusion contested by Webb et al., who say newer models generalise.
agent_relevance: Treat analogy benchmarks with familiar content as upper bounds. Any transfer test for our schema must use unfamiliar surface forms (G3).

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 are brittle on counterfactual letter-string variants (permuted or symbol alphabets) while humans are robust. On digit matrices, moving the blank position breaks GPT but not humans. On story analogies GPT-4 shows answer-order bias and more sensitivity to paraphrase.
numbers: Digit matrices mean accuracy: humans 0.715 original, 0.771 alt blank, 0.704 symbols (N=1,550 / 1,000 / 1,000 samples); GPT-3.5 0.813 -> 0.480 alt blank; GPT-4 0.810 -> 0.477 (row labels read from garbled layout, so model order is inferred). Story analogies, 18 far-analogy items: GPT-4 correct-first 0.89 (16/18) vs correct-second 0.61 (11/18); humans 0.78 vs 0.78. Paraphrased correct answer: GPT-4 0.86 -> 0.72 (26/36), humans drop less; only 18 items, low power.
limits: Letter-string results are in figures. Newer reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Models can fail on a structurally identical task when only the surface layout changes. Our held-out checks should vary surface form (G3).

source: Stevenson et al. (2024) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Adults and children transfer a letter-string rule from Latin to Greek (near) and symbol (far) alphabets without loss; LLMs lose accuracy as the domain gets less familiar.
numbers: Mean accuracy Latin / Greek / Symbol: adults (n=62) 0.88 / 0.91 / 0.89; children (n=41) 0.62 / 0.66 / 0.67; Claude-3.5 0.68 / 0.62 / 0.46; Gemma-2 27B 0.60 / 0.39 / 0.14; GPT-4o 0.85 / 0.63 / 0.48; Llama-3.1 405B 0.79 / 0.74 / 0.27. Claude-3.5 does well on a next/previous-letter knowledge check in all three alphabets yet still degrades on the far-transfer analogy.
limits: Letter-string rules only; five items per alphabet. No scaffold was tried.
agent_relevance: Even with the component knowledge intact, models do not carry the abstract rule across surface domains. Abstraction must be made explicit and tested in a new domain.

source: Puranam, Sen and Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs Help Improve Analogical Reasoning For Strategic Decisions? Experimental Evidence from Humans and GPT-4
finding: Gick and Holyoak style test with two source stories (radiation, dolphins) and two target problems (factory, HR). GPT-4 retrieves analogies freely but applies the wrong one by surface features; humans are conservative but precise.
numbers: Humans N=199 (46 per target condition): factory problem solved 6.3% no hint, 8.7% with hint; HR problem 20.3% no hint, 37% with hint (original Gick and Holyoak 1983 Exp 2: 29% (8/28) no hint, 50% (14/28) with hint). GPT-4, 15 trials per cell: radiation analogy used 1/15 without hint, 15/15 with hint; dolphin 14/15 without hint. With hint GPT-4 recall 1.00, precision about 0.50-0.52, F1 0.67-0.68; humans precision 0.67-0.75, recall 0.26-0.39. Without hint GPT-4 never picked the correct source (precision, recall, F1 = 0).
limits: Management-style problems, small LLM sample, one model, preprint. Tests matching, not schema induction from several cases.
agent_relevance: Having several candidate cases in context does not give a schema; the model applies whichever looks similar. Matching must be checked against causal structure, not wording (G3, G4).

source: Wang et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: Ask the model for several natural-language hypotheses about the rule behind examples, implement each as a program, and test it against the examples. Abstract rule first, code second.
numbers: ARC 100-task sample, GPT-4: direct prompting 17%; programs without hypotheses 23%; programs with LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%; with human-selected LLM hypotheses 33%; human-written hypotheses (LARC) about 33%; non-LLM DSL search (Icecuber) 43%. Chain-of-thought with hypotheses but no programs: 19%. 49 tasks with selected hypotheses: 33 (67%) correct programs.
limits: ARC subset of 100; GPT-4 of 2023. Gain depends on the program-execution check, not the hypothesis text alone.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'propose abstract rule, then verify by running' (G2, G3). The natural-language rule alone adds almost nothing; the check does the work.

source: Wang et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: Other domains: more hypotheses and programs help up to a point; hypotheses plus programs do not always beat plain two-shot prompting.
numbers: SyGuS 94.3% with 4 hypotheses x 2 programs; list functions 71.3% with 16 hypotheses x 4 programs vs 73.1% with two-shot prompting; GPT-3.5 reaches 27% with 128 programs and 30% with feedback (GPT-4 higher, GPT-3.5 about 20x cheaper).
limits: Budgets differ per domain, so cross-task comparison is loose.
agent_relevance: Spend budget per problem (G12); abstraction is not a universal win.

source: Parab, Lu, Wu and Gulwani (2025) Analysis of Error Sources in LLM-based Hypothesis Search for Few-Shot Rule Induction
finding: On 100 list-function induction tasks, hypothesis search reaches human-like learning curves while direct program generation lags. The main bottleneck is the hypothesis generator.
numbers: Modules: Hypothesis Generator 46.4% correct, Summarizer 34.5%, Program Implementor 61.2%. Overall test solve rate 62.0%. Summarizing drops 26% of correct generator hypotheses (12.1 points absolute loss). Implementor rescues 19.9% of trials (37.0% of double-failure at front end); refinement fixed only 4.3% of semantically wrong hypotheses.
limits: Simple list functions, one pipeline, preprint. Human comparison given as curves; no exact human percent recorded here.
agent_relevance: Names two failure points for our schema: a good rule is lost in summarising, and the generator is the limit.

source: Parab et al. (2025) hypothesis search error analysis: false passes
finding: Passing the shown examples is weak proof of the right rule.
numbers: 'Nearly half of the programs that passed this test (45.4%) failed against the ground-truth' check.
limits: One task family.
agent_relevance: Backs G3: a pass on the fitted examples is not proof; test on held-out inputs.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: An LLM web agent induces reusable workflows (abstracted sub-routines with example-specific values replaced by placeholders) from past successful episodes and adds them to memory. Gains grow as the train-test gap widens.
numbers: WebArena: +12.0 absolute and +51.1% relative success rate over the BrowserGym baseline; +7.6% relative over SteP with human-written workflows. Mind2Web +24.6% relative step success. Across 5 sites +11.8 to +30.7 absolute. Cross-task/website/domain gains of 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as the gap widens. LM-induced vs rule-induced workflows (gpt-4): 35.5 vs 35.6 success, 5.9 vs 6.3 steps.
limits: Rule-based induction (deduplicate action sequences) matches the LM method on success, so much of the gain is simply reusing validated past routines. Induction uses only successes; web tasks only.
agent_relevance: A working method inside an agent loop: abstract from solved cases, store, retrieve. The cheap rule-based version gets nearly all the gain, supporting induction in code.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: ExpeL collects success and failure trajectories, then an LLM compares success/failure pairs on the same task (and lists of successes) to write general insights using ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE. This is analogical encoding in an agent loop.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only success: HotpotQA 36% / 31%; ALFWorld 50% / 55%; WebShop 37% / 38%; both together best. ExpeL matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% at R3 vs 39%). Agent-written insights beat human-crafted ones; adding reflections to the pair comparison hurt (hallucinated reflections); a better extractor model (gpt-4 vs gpt-3.5) helped. An agent with only the starter few-shot examples (no success/failure pairs) gained nothing over ReAct.
limits: Gains depend on having gathered success/failure pairs. Some table cells garbled in text extraction, so transfer-to-FEVER numbers are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Closest agent-loop analogue of Loewenstein-style comparison: compare a failure with a success on the same task, then write a rule. Needs real failures and successes, supporting G2.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025/ICLR 2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Agent distils strategy-level memory items from its own successes and failures (judged by the model itself), retrieves them on new tasks, and uses extra attempts at test time (MaTTS) to get contrastive signal.
numbers: WebArena success (no memory / Synapse / AWM / ReasoningBank): Gemini-2.5-flash 40.5 / 42.1 / 44.1 / 48.8; Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7 / 47.7 / 47.6 / 53.9; Claude-3.7-sonnet 41.7 / 42.6 / 40.8 / 46.3. SWE-Bench-Verified: flash 34.2 -> 38.8, pro 54.0 -> 57.4. Adding failures (Shopping, flash): Synapse 40.6 -> 41.7, AWM 44.4 -> 42.2, ReasoningBank 46.5 -> 49.7. MaTTS k=1 -> 5: parallel 49.7 -> 55.1, sequential 49.7 -> 54.5.
limits: Read through a summarised fetch of the HTML (tables transcribed by the fetch tool). Success labels come from an LLM judge, which clashes with G5. Mind2Web gains tiny in absolute terms (3.3 -> 4.8).
agent_relevance: Abstracting from failures as well as successes adds value, and more attempts sharpen the contrast. The self-judged success label is the weak point; use code checks instead.

source: McLure, Friedman and Forbus (2015) Extending Analogical Generalization with Near-Misses (ALIGN)
finding: ALIGN builds on SAGE (structure-mapping generalisation) and also retrieves its own near-miss cases (similar cases with different labels), turning the differences into hypotheses that block the wrong label. Beats generalisation without near-misses on two datasets.
numbers: Exp 1 (44 sketches, 6 labels, 16 null-label near-misses, 4-fold CV, chance 21%): Examples 55%, Prototypes (SAGE only) 55%, ALIGN 62% (+7, p<0.01). Exp 2 (60 geospatial examples, 6 categories, 10-fold CV): ALIGN peak 77%, Prototypes peak 62%, Examples 53% (p<0.05). Best similarity threshold about 0.8.
limits: Symbolic sketch descriptions, tiny datasets, one-tailed paired t-tests. SAGE alone gave no gain over storing examples in experiment 1.
agent_relevance: A computable recipe: compare similar cases with different outcomes and keep only differences that survive more comparisons. Useful for code-level induction of what separates passing from failing attempts.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with LLMs
finding: Templates narrow the gap between a small and a large model on structured tasks.
numbers: BoT with Llama3-70B: Game of 24 78.4, Checkmate-in-One 75.6, word sorting 92.3. Llama3-70B alone on Game of 24 is 2.4 and Llama3-8B alone 1.2; BoT+Llama3-8B approaches or passes unaided Llama3-70B.
limits: Read from figure text, so 8B BoT values are approximate. Narrow task families.
agent_relevance: Library-based scaffold adds most for weaker models; test whether a stronger model needs it at all (G7).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Generating background knowledge before examples helps harder tasks more than easy ones; self-consistency can be stacked on top.
numbers: Codeforces: GPT-3.5-turbo with 15% Acc@1 reaches GPT-4's 16%. Knowledge gains are smaller on GSM8K and BIG-bench.
limits: Acc@1 differences of 1 to 2 points on a hard benchmark may be noise.
agent_relevance: Use only on hard, knowledge-heavy problems; skip on easy ones to save tokens (G11, G12).
